PLS regression; mixOmics scales every channel by default, scale = FALSE # only centers them pls_model <- pls(num_comp = tune()) |>   set_mode("regression") |>   set_engine("mixOmics", scale = FALSE)  # A recipe for one log-ratio: the channels are predictors, the other # targets are identifiers logratio_recipe <- function(data, outcome) {   recipe(data) |>     update_role(all_of(channels), new_role = "predictor") |>     update_role(all_of(outcome), new_role = "outcome") |>     update_role(Sample, clay, any_of(setdiff(c("clay_silt", "sand_silt"), outcome)),                 new_role = "id") }  # The same split, on another table with the samples in the same order reindex <- function(split, data) {   make_splits(list(analysis = split$in_id, assessment = complement(split)), data = data) }  # Number of components minimizing the inner-CV error of the back-transformed # clay predictions, from the two log-ratio workflows and their inner resamples select_ncomp <- function(workflows, inner_sets, cal) {   predictions <- map2(workflows, inner_sets, \(wf, inner) {     tune_grid(wf, resamples = inner, grid = tibble(num_comp = 1:10),               control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE)) |>       collect_predictions() |>       select(.row, num_comp, .pred)   })   inner_join(predictions$clay_silt, predictions$sand_silt,              by = c(".row", "num_comp"), suffix = c("_1", "_2")) |>     mutate(error = back_transform(.pred_1, .pred_2) - cal$clay[.row]) |>     group_by(num_comp) |>     summarise(rmse = sqrt(mean(error^2))) |>     slice_min(rmse, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>     pull(num_comp) }  # One outer split: tune on the calibration part, predict the held-out part. # `pipeline` holds the data (or one table per log-ratio), optional recipe # steps and, optionally, a fixed number of components. evaluate_split <- function(pipeline, split, inner) {   outcomes <- c(clay_silt = "clay_silt", sand_silt = "sand_silt")   data_for <- function(outcome) {     if (is.data.frame(pipeline$data)) pipeline$data else pipeline$data[[outcome]]   }   splits <- map(outcomes, \(o) reindex(split, data_for(o)))   cal <- analysis(splits$clay_silt)   workflows <- map(outcomes, \(o) {     rec <- logratio_recipe(analysis(splits[[o]]), o)     if (!is.null(pipeline$steps)) rec <- pipeline$steps(rec, cal$Sample)     workflow(rec, pls_model)   })   ncomp <- pipeline$ncomp   if (is.null(ncomp)) {     inner_sets <- map(outcomes, \(o) manual_rset(       map(inner$splits, \(s) reindex(s, analysis(splits[[o]]))), inner$id))     ncomp <- select_ncomp(workflows, inner_sets, cal)   }   predicted <- map2(workflows, outcomes, \(wf, o) {     finalize_workflow(wf, tibble(num_comp = ncomp)) |>       fit(data = analysis(splits[[o]])) |>       predict(new_data = assessment(splits[[o]])) |>       pull(.pred)   })   tibble(Sample = assessment(splits$clay_silt)$Sample,          clay = assessment(splits$clay_silt)$clay,          pred = back_transform(predicted$clay_silt, predicted$sand_silt),          ncomp = ncomp) }  # Repeated nested CV of a pipeline cross_validate <- function(pipeline, folds) {   folds |>     mutate(result = map2(splits, inner_resamples, \(s, i) evaluate_split(pipeline, s, i))) |>     select(-splits, -inner_resamples) |>     rename(repeat_id = id) |>     unnest(result) }

code: icc <- function(v, group) {   # constant (up to rounding) within the data: no variance to decompose   if (stats::sd(v) <= 1e-8 * abs(mean(v))) return(NA_real_)   fit <- stats::anova(stats::lm(v ~ factor(group)))   k <- mean(table(group))   msb <- fit[1, "Mean Sq"]   msw <- fit[2, "Mean Sq"]   (msb - msw) / (msb + (k - 1) * msw) } rsd <- function(v, group) {   median(tapply(v, group, function(z) sd(z) / mean(z) * 100)) } normalized <- function(step, ...) {   baseline_recipe(specLIBS, 1e5) |>     step(all_predictors(), ...) |>     prep() |>     bake(new_data = NULL) } candidates <- list(   `baseline only` = baselined,   `area` = bind_cols(select(baselined, Sample),                      normalize(baselined[channels], method = "area")),   `SNV` = normalized(step_snv),   `MSC` = normalized(step_msc),   `internal std. title: Preprocessing Tools for Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS) Spectra
text: specProc R package preprocessing exploring emission spectra, focus laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS). covers full chain raw detector counts data matrix ready modeling: Baseline correction: asymmetric least squares, arPLS, iterative polynomial fitting. Normalization scaling: SNV, MSC, extended MSC (EMSC), area, background internal-standard normalization; Pareto, Poisson min-max scaling. Removing unwanted variation: OSC (three algorithms), direct orthogonalization, DOSC, O2PLS, projected OSC, EPO, GLSW. Robust PCA: ROBPCA, robust sparse PCA (ROSPCA) MacroPCA, outlier maps cell maps. Figures merit: net analyte signal, sensitivity, selectivity, analytical sensitivity, limits detection quantification. tidymodels integration: recipe steps baseline correction, SNV, MSC, EMSC, scaling every orthogonalization filter, preprocessing re-estimated resample tuned model. Calibration transfer instruments: PDS, GLSW. Line fitting: exact Voigt, pseudo-Voigt, Gaussian Lorentzian profiles, single overlapping lines. Plasma diagnostics: electron density Stark broadening, widths STARK-B database, H-alpha; temperature Boltzmann Saha-Boltzmann plots; McWhirter criterion, self-absorption detector saturation. Robust statistics outlier detection: biweight estimators, Rousseeuw–Croux Sn/Qn, bias-corrected MAD, medcouple-based skewness tail weights, adjusted generalized boxplots, directional outlyingness. computationally heavy steps written C++: penalized baselines use banded solver, Voigt profile uses Faddeeva function, large matrix decompositions use Eigen. keeps package practical data sets thousands spectra channels.

code: # Simulated lines of a plasma at 9000 K with 70% Fe and 30% Ca (atomic # fractions), with made-up atomic data and partition functions kB <- 8.617333262e-5 T <- 9000 U <- function(species, temperature) c("Fe I" = 30, "Fe II" = 40, "Ca I" = 3, "Ca II" = 2)[species] lines <- data.frame(   species = c("Fe I", "Fe I", "Fe I", "Fe II", "Fe II", "Ca I", "Ca I", "Ca II"),   wavelength = c(371, 404, 438, 259, 275, 422, 445, 393),   Aki = c(1.6e7, 8.6e7, 5.0e7, 2.2e8, 2.1e8, 2.2e8, 8.7e7, 1.5e8),   gk = c(11, 9, 11, 10, 8, 3, 7, 4),   Ek = c(3.33, 4.55, 4.31, 4.77, 5.55, 2.93, 4.68, 3.15) ) # number densities of each species, in arbitrary units n <- c("Fe I" = 0.70 * 0.2, "Fe II" = 0.70 * 0.8, "Ca I" = 0.30 * 0.05, "Ca II" = 0.30 * 0.95) set.seed(1)  # 5% measurement noise lines$intensity <- with(lines, n[species] / U(species) * gk * Aki / wavelength *   exp(-Ek / (kB * T)) * exp(rnorm(8, sd = 0.05))) fit <- cf_libs(lines, partition = U) fit #> Calibration-free LIBS (8 lines, 4 species; Boltzmann plots) #>  #> Temperature:  9132 +/- 173 K #> Normalization: closure #>  #>  element atomic_fraction mass_fraction stages #>  Fe      0.6930          0.7588        I, II  #>  Ca      0.3070          0.2412        I, II  plot_boltzmann(fit)

title: Net Analyte Signal and Figures of Merit — nas
text: net analyte signal part spectrum unique analyte, .e. orthogonal spectral contributions constituents (interferents). inverse calibration model \(\hat{y} = \bar{y} + (\textbf{x} - \bar{\textbf{x}})^T\textbf{b}\) \(\) latent variables, interferent space spanned calibration spectra reconstructed model, part explained \(\hat{\textbf{y}}\) removed. regression vector \(\textbf{b}\) orthogonal space, NAS space within model one-dimensional spanned \(\textbf{b}\) (Faber, 1998; Bro Andersen, 2003). NAS vector sample \(\) therefore $$\textbf{r}_i^* = \frac{(\textbf{x}_i - \bar{\textbf{x}})^T\textbf{b}}{\|\textbf{b}\|^2}\,\textbf{b}$$ signed length, scalar NAS, $$\mathrm{NAS}_i = \frac{(\textbf{x}_i - \bar{\textbf{x}})^T\textbf{b}}{\|\textbf{b}\|} = \frac{\hat{y}_i - \bar{y}}{\|\textbf{b}\|}$$ figures merit follow Olivieri et al. (2006): Sensitivity, \(\mathrm{SEN} = 1 / \|\textbf{b}\|\): NAS produced unit change concentration, signal units per concentration unit. Selectivity sample \(\), \(\mathrm{SEL}_i = |\mathrm{NAS}_i| / \|\textbf{x}_i - \bar{\textbf{x}}\|\): fraction (centered) signal used prediction, 0 1. standard deviation instrumental noise \(\sigma_x\) (noise): analytical sensitivity \(\gamma = \mathrm{SEN} / \sigma_x\), whose inverse smallest concentration difference can distinguished; limit detection \(\mathrm{LOD} = 3.3\,\sigma_x / \mathrm{SEN}\); limit quantification \(\mathrm{LOQ} = 10\,\sigma_x / \mathrm{SEN}\); signal--noise ratio sample, \(\mathrm{NAS}_i / \sigma_x\). LOD LOQ account instrumental noise , uncertainty calibration model reference values, lower bounds. noise level must estimated independently, example standard deviation differences repeated spectra sample divided \(\sqrt{2}\), units (preprocessing) x. quantities depend number latent variables ncomp, chosen validation beforehand. specProc 0.4.0, nas() returned spectra filtered direct orthogonalization; correction available direct_orthogonal().

code: # Three constituents with overlapping lines; the analyte is the first one set.seed(1) wl <- seq(390, 400, length.out = 200) line <- function(center) exp(-(wl - center)^2 / 0.1) pure <- rbind(line(393.4) + 0.3 * line(396.8), line(393.8), line(396.5)) conc <- matrix(runif(30 * 3, 0, 1), 30, 3) x <- conc %*% pure + matrix(rnorm(30 * 200, sd = 0.002), 30)  fit <- nas(x, conc[, 1], ncomp = 3, noise = 0.002) fit #> Net analyte signal (PLS model, 3 components) #>  #> Calibration samples:     30 #> Sensitivity:             2.59 #> Mean selectivity:        0.565 #> Noise (sd):              0.002 #> Analytical sensitivity:  1295 #> LOD:                     0.002548 #> LOQ:                     0.007722 head(fit$nas) #> # A tibble: 6 × 4 #>      nas selectivity fitted    snr #>    <dbl>       <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> #> 1 -0.633       0.510  0.265 -317.  #> 2 -0.358       0.460  0.371 -179.  #> 3  0.164       0.803  0.573   82.1 #> 4  1.03        0.895  0.908  516.  #> 5 -0.795       0.829  0.202 -398.  #> 6  1.01        0.692  0.898  503.   # the sensitivity equals the length of the analyte spectrum orthogonal # to the interferent spectra interf <- t(pure[2:3, ]) net <- pure[1, ] - interf %*% qr.solve(interf, pure[1, ]) c(model = fit$figures_of_merit[["sensitivity"]], theory = sqrt(sum(net^2))) #>    model   theory  #> 2.590138 2.591504

Voigt profile evaluated exactly C++; pseudo-Voigt (Thompson-Cox-Hastings) approximation faster accurate 1\ Initial values supplied estimated data: peak center position maximum, width full width half maximum, area integrated intensity minimum. center constrained fitted wavelength range widths area positive values. fit spectrum fails, warning issued corresponding fit, tidied augmented entries NULL.

title: Peak Fitting — peak_fit

title: Pseudo-Voigt Function — pseudo_voigt_profile

title: Pseudo-Voigt Function — pseudo_voigt_profile
text: x numeric vector representing independent variable (e.g., wavelength frequency). y0 numeric value specifying baseline offset. xc numeric value representing center peak. wG numeric value specifying Gaussian full width half maximum (FWHM). wL numeric value specifying Lorentzian FWHM. numeric value representing peak area. eta numeric value 0 1, representing mixing parameter. eta = NULL (default), mixing parameter approximated polynomial function wG wL. approximation (accuracy 1%), proposed Ida et al. (2000), provides analytical expression mixing parameter based relative FWHM Gaussian Lorentzian components. polynomial approximation useful precise value eta unknown.

title: Pseudo-Voigt Function — pseudo_voigt_profile
text: numeric vector length x, containing computed pseudo-Voigt function values. eta = NULL, function returns list following components: $y: numeric vector length x, containing computed pseudo-Voigt function values using approximated mixing parameter. $eta: approximate mixing parameter calculated using polynomial approximation based wG wL values.

title: Pseudo-Voigt Function — pseudo_voigt_profile
text: Pseudo-Voigt function given : $$y = y_0 + \cdot [ \eta \cdot L(x, x_c, w_L) + (1 - \eta) \cdot G(x, x_c, w_G)]$$ : \(\) peak area \(y_0\) baseline offset \(G(x, x_c, w_G)\) Gaussian component center \(x_c\) full width half maximum \(w_G\) \(L(x, x_c, w_L)\) Lorentzian component center \(x_c\) full width half maximum \(w_L\) \(\eta\) mixing parameter, \(0 \leq \eta \leq 1\). mixing parameter \(\eta\) allows pseudo-Voigt function describe wide range line shapes, pure Gaussian (\(\eta = 0\)) pure Lorentzian (\(\eta = 1\)), various intermediate shapes . \(G\) \(L\) unit area, \(\) area peak. eta given, Thompson-Cox-Hastings approximation Voigt profile used (Ida et al. 2000): components share total FWHM $$f = (w_G^5 + 2.69269 w_G^4 w_L + 2.42843 w_G^3 w_L^2 + 4.47163 w_G^2 w_L^3 + 0.07842 w_G w_L^4 + w_L^5)^{1/5}$$ mixing parameter $$\eta = 1.36603 (w_L/f) - 0.47719 (w_L/f)^2 + 0.11116 (w_L/f)^3$$ comparison, Olivero Longbothum (1977) approximation, subsequent refinements (Belafhal 2000; Zdunkowski et al. 2007), estimate FWHM Voigt line \(w_V = \frac{1}{2} [c_1 w_L + \sqrt{c_2 w_L^2 + 4 w_G^2}]\) \(c_1 = 1.0692\), \(c_2 = 0.86639\) (accuracy 0.02%).

title: Pseudo-Voigt Function — pseudo_voigt_profile
text: Zdunkowski, W., Trautmann, T., Bott, ., (2007). Radiation Atmosphere — Course Theoretical Meteorology. Cambridge University Press. Belafhal, ., (2000). shape spectral lines: Widths equivalent widths Voigt profile. Opt. Commun., 177(1-6):111–118. Olivero, J., Longbothum, R., (1977). Empirical fits Voigt line width: brief review. J. Quant. Spectrosc. Radiat. Transfer, 17(2):233–236. Ida, T., Ando, M., Toraya, H., (2000). Extended pseudo-Voigt function approximating Voigt profile. Journal Applied Crystallography. 33(6):1311–1316.

title: Pseudo-Voigt Function — pseudo_voigt_profile

title: Quantile Tail Weight Measure — quantile_weight
text: quantile weights, comprising left quantile weight (LQW) right quantile weight (RQW), robust measures tail weight probability distributions. breakdown value 12.5%, meaning resistant influence 12.5% outliers contaminated data. concept quantile weights derived quartile skewness, introduced D.V. Hinkley 1975. Quartile skewness measures skewness asymmetry distribution comparing differences quartiles, robust measures location scale. Specifically, quantile weights obtained applying quartile skewness either left half right half probability mass, divided median univariate distribution (Brys et al. 2006): $$LQW(p) = -\frac{Q((1-p)/2) + Q(p/2) - 2Q(0.25)}{Q((1-p)/2) - Q(p/2)}$$ $$RQW(q) = \frac{Q((1+q)/2) + Q(1-q/2) - 2Q(0.75)}{Q((1+q)/2) - Q(1-q/2)}$$ \(Q\) quantile function data. defaults \(p = 0.125\) \(q = 0.875\) give breakdown value 12.5%. Interpretation Quantile Weights: normal distribution, LQW = RQW ≈ 0.2. Larger values indicate heavier tails normal distribution, smaller values lighter tails.

STARK-B fits widths shifts given perturber density $$\log w = a_0 + a_1 \log T + a_2 (\log T)^2$$ $$d / w = b_0 + b_1 \log T + b_2 (\log T)^2$$ decimal logarithms \(w\) units tables (Å); fits valid within tabulated temperature range (Sahal-Bréchot, Dimitrijević Ben Nessib, 2011). coefficients, table evaluated temperature, span range. code: # made-up widths of a hypothetical line, in Angstrom at 1e17 cm-3 x <- stark_table(   wavelength = 5000, temperature = c(5000, 10000, 20000),   width = c(0.20, 0.16, 0.13), units = "A", species = "X II" ) x #> # A tibble: 3 × 10 #>   species wavelength upper lower perturber temperature density width shift #>   <chr>        <dbl> <chr> <chr> <chr>           <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 X II           500 ""    ""    electron         5000    1e17 0.02      0 #> 2 X II           500 ""    ""    electron        10000    1e17 0.016     0 #> 3 X II           500 ""    ""    electron        20000    1e17 0.013     0 #> # ℹ 1 more variable: source <chr> electron_density(0.012, stark = x, wavelength = 500, temperature = 8000) #> [1] 6.980125e+16  # the same line from the coefficients of a fitted temperature law # log10(w) = a0 + a1 log10(T) + a2 log10(T)^2 (here fitted to the table above) lt <- log10(c(5000, 10000, 20000)) a <- unname(coef(lm(log10(c(0.20, 0.16, 0.13)) ~ lt + I(lt^2)))) stark_table(wavelength = 5000, temperature = c(5000, 10000, 20000),             coefficients = a, units = "A") #> # A tibble: 3 × 10 #>   species wavelength upper lower perturber temperature density  width shift #>   <chr>        <dbl> <chr> <chr> <chr>           <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 NA             500 ""    ""    electron         5000    1e17 0.0200     0 #> 2 NA             500 ""    ""    electron        10000    1e17 0.016      0 #> 3 NA             500 ""    ""    electron        20000    1e17 0.013      0 #> # ℹ 1 more variable: source <chr>

title: Tukey g-and-h Parametric Distribution — tukey_gh
text: Tukey g--h distribution, introduced John W. Tukey 1977, defined two transformation functions, g h, applied standard normal distribution. g transformation controls skewness distribution, h transformation controls kurtosis (heaviness tails). TGH distribution given : $$T_{g,h}(Z) = \frac{1}{g} (e^{g Z} -1) e^{\frac{1}{2} h Z^2}$$ \(Z\) random variable standard normal distribution. parameters \(g\) \(h\) stand bias elongation tails, respectively, Tukey’s \(g\)--\(h\) distribution.

title: Voigt Function — voigt_profile
text: Computes exact Voigt profile, convolution Gaussian Lorentzian profile. laser-induced plasmas, Gaussian component typically reflects Doppler instrumental broadening, Lorentzian component Stark (pressure) natural broadening.

title: Voigt Function — voigt_profile
code: voigt_profile(x, y0, xc, wG, wL, A)

title: Voigt Function — voigt_profile
text: x numeric vector representing independent variable (e.g., wavelength). y0 numeric value specifying baseline offset. xc numeric value representing center peak. wG non-negative numeric value specifying Gaussian full width half maximum (FWHM). wL non-negative numeric value specifying Lorentzian FWHM. numeric value representing peak area.

title: Voigt Function — voigt_profile
text: numeric vector containing values Voigt function evaluated provided x values.

title: Voigt Function — voigt_profile
text: Voigt function defined : $$y = y_0 + \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} G(t; w_G)\, L(x - x_c - t; w_L)\, dt = y_0 + \frac{\mathrm{Re}[w(z)]}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}, \quad z = \frac{x - x_c + \gamma}{\sigma\sqrt{2}}$$ \(w(z) = e^{-z^2}\mathrm{erfc}(-iz)\) Faddeeva function, \(\sigma = w_G / (2\sqrt{2\ln 2})\) standard deviation Gaussian component \(\gamma = w_L / 2\) half width half maximum Lorentzian component. components unit area, \(\) area line. Faddeeva function evaluated C++ Weideman's (1994) rational approximation using 32 terms. relative error \(10^{-10}\) range widths met emission spectroscopy. width zero gives pure Gaussian pure Lorentzian profile. See pseudo_voigt_profile() faster pseudo-Voigt approximation.

title: Voigt Function — voigt_profile
text: Weideman, J..C., (1994). Computation complex error function. SIAM Journal Numerical Analysis, 31(5):1497-1518. Armstrong, B.H., (1967). Spectrum line profiles: Voigt function. J. Quant. Spectrosc. Radiat. Transfer, 7(1):61-88.

text: tibble containing \(p \times p\) filtering matrix.

title: y-Gradient Generalized Least Squares Weighting — y_gradient_glsw
text: y-Gradient GLSW alternative method GLSW, continuous \(\textbf{y}\)-variable used develop pseudo-groupings samples \(\textbf{X}\) comparing differences corresponding \(\textbf{y}\) values. referred "gradient method" utilizes gradient sorted \(\textbf{X}\)- \(\textbf{y}\)-blocks calculate covariance matrix. samples sorted increasing \(\textbf{y}\), first derivatives \(\textbf{X}\) \(\textbf{y}\) along sample axis computed Savitzky-Golay filter. Samples whose neighbors similar \(\textbf{y}\) values receive large weights \(w_i = 2^{-\Delta y_i / s_{\Delta y}}\), differences spectra, \(\Delta\textbf{X}\), describe variation unrelated \(\textbf{y}\). filter built glsw() \(\textbf{C} = \Delta\textbf{X}^T\textbf{W}^2\Delta\textbf{X}\).

title: Classical or Robust Z-Score — zscore
text: Z-scores useful comparing data points different distributions dimensionless standardized. positive z-score indicates data point mean (median robust approach), negative z-score indicates data point mean (median). One common rule detect outliers using z-scores "three-sigma rule", data points absolute z-score greater 3 (|z| > 3) can considered potential outliers (default), fall outside range covers 99.7% data points normal distribution. (Note cutoff |z| > 2.5 also often used).
